maintopic: LOAN OF $750,000,000 TO MEET LOANS OR OBLIGATIONS, TO PURCHASE UNMATURED SECURITIES, AND FOR GENERAL PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, nothing affects the economic welfare of our country more than our money policy. We have contended that our monetary system must reflect the country's collective ability to produce and distribute goods and services for the people of Canada. The borrowing of this $750,000,000 will affect every man, woman and child living in Canada to-day, and it will affect also the lives of every man, woman and child who may live in Canada in the years to come. We maintain that our monetary system must be corrected if civilization is to progress. Every time we make a proposal the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) raises the issue of inflation, but I should like to refer to a statement by the minister as reported on page 1527 of Hansard of March 3, 1939, as follows:
My hon. friends deny on all occasions that they advocate inflation, but they propose resolutions similar in terms to the one we now have before us, which does mean the issue of currency by the Bank of Canada to the extent of from $500,000,000 to $750,000,000 more currency than is now outstanding, which would mean an increase in the total currency available in thip country of from two and a half to four and a half times. Now, my hon. friend says he does not advocate inflation.
I say once more that we do not advocate inflation. It is well to remember that the provincial debt, the municipal debt and the national debt are all increasing. In 1912 the net debt of Canada was $339,919,461. In 1913 it was $314,301,625 and in 1914, $335,996,850. At that time the debt was approximately equal to the amount of currency available in the country, tout to-day our debt is atoout eighteen times greater than the amount of currency in circulation. Our provincial debt in 1925 was $813,400,000, about five times greater than all the currency available in circulation. By 1935 this had risen to $1,622,100,000, or albout ten times greater than all the currency available in circulation. In 1926 the municipal debt was $1,050,206,121, or six times greater than all the currency in circulation. By 1935 this had risen to $1,452,850,565 or nine times greater than all the currency in circulation. So our total

municipal, provincial and federal debt is many times greater than all the currency available in circulation.
Considering the tremendous inflation which has occurred in the debt of the country, it is hardly right to say that the issue of $600,000,000 would be inflation. I suggested that the government should issue $600,000,000. This issue would be without cost to the government, apart from the cost of printing. But what was the answer of the Minister of Finance? His answer was in these words:
An increase of say $350,000,000 in chartered bank holdings of Bank of Canada notes would increase their cash reserves from the present figure of about $250,000,000 to $600,000,000, and their cash ratio from about ten per cent to roughly twenty-four per cent. The sponsor of the suggestion contends that no inflation is intended or would result by thus increasing bank cash, so long as the gold cover of the Bank of Canada did not fall below the twenty-five per cent minimum. This factor, however, is not a test of inflation. If the banks use their increased cash in a normal way, as a basis for the extension of roughly ten times as much in loans to the public, or for the acquisition of ten times as much in investments, bank deposits would expand by approximately an equal amount until the cash ratio was brought down again to approximately ten per cent.
If instead of issuing bonds and having the bankers create credit out of nothing, as we have done in the past, the government would issue $600,000,000, under our present banking laws it would mean inflation. If the banks were permitted to take $600,000,000 worth of cash and expand credit ten to one, it would mean an increase of $6,000,000,000 in the credit of this country. That is provided there were borrowers who would be prepared to take the money. Our banks cannot always get rid of their surplus credit, and this would depend upon whether or not there were borrowers ready to borrow from the banks. At the present time it must be remembered that our banks have only ten per cent cash reserve. Time and time again the government have said that they have control of the issue of currency and credit day by day, week by week and month by month. If the government takes action and forces the banks to increase their cash reserves, takes action to prevent the banks from inflating credit, then there would not be one dollar's worth of credit expansion in this country. The Minister of Finance knows that full well.

speechtext: Positively yes. But, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take the time of this committee once more, as I have on three different occasions when my hon. friend and his associates have cross-examined me, to go into an elaborate discussion of the basis of our banking laws and banking system. I tried to meet that demand and to save the time of the house by moving in the house that the report of the Bank of Canada be referred to the banking and commerce committee, to the end that all members of the house who desired it might in the banking committee have the privilege of cross-questioning not only myself, if they wanted me, but also the officers of the bank and the officers of the department. No one can say that there has not been ample opportunity in the house this session for the ventilation of views on the question of monetary policy. I do not propose this afternoon again to go into detailed technical argument, as I did before, on this question, because it is being carried on very effectively in another and more appropriate place. I rise only when my hon. friend makes a statement which at a critical time like this might possibly weaken the confidence of the Canadian people who have their money on deposit in Canadian banks. There are four million depositors, and I am very much more concerned about them than about my hon. friend's argument. That is the only reason I rise, when he attempts to put forward the idea that there is some lack of security with respect to the deposits of the Canadian people in the chartered banks. In my opinion the Canadian banking system as now operated through the control exercised by the central bank, is in a more secure position in relation to its depositors than it has ever been before in the whole history of Canada.

Later, in an interview with the press Mr. Dunning emphatically stated that his chief concern was to preserve intact the credit of the dominion and that political considerations were entirely absent from the communications

The paper prints circles showing the amount of debt of the city of Montreal, and the percentages. It says that the present total bonded debt of all rural municipalities is $558,736,888.
This circle presents the most tragic^ picture in the financial, economic and constitutional history of the province of Quebec. The farming communities of our province are mostly dominated and subjugated by crushing debts imposed upon them by the politicians of the federal governments at Ottawa. The above amounts and percentages have increased considerably since the year 1936. All amounts given in the above chart are taken from official returns of the fiscal year 1936.
This illustrates the crushing weight of the tremendous burden of debt which is being piled up by this federal government. The mayors of the dominion are meeting now to discuss their problems-

Neither the amendment I moved the other day nor the amendment I now propose is part of a social credit scheme; it is simply a proposal recognizing that something must be done about the tremendous debt burden that the country is now carrying. It simply means that whatever funds the government intends to spend on public works and for general purposes shall be raised "by the said issue of currency." It may amount to $100,000,000. Under the present scheme, as I understand it, the government intends to borrow the money by selling bonds or securities. Those bonds and securities are issued against the word of the people of Canada. We ask the government to raise in the same way, the amount required, against the word or the credit of the people of Canada. And this money would be spent in the same way as money would be spent if derived from the sale of securities.
I do not fear that this proposal, if adopted, would give rise to inflation. I simply say that it would be a step in the right direction, fulfilling the Liberal promise to issue money and credit in terms of public need. There is need now for public works and the money that will be expended is for that purpose. If proper steps are taken to ensure adequate control over the issue of credit, there will be no danger of inflation.

Speaking to the point of order, I do not think the position taken by the Minister of Finance is well taken. The point of order is not to decide whether or not parliament is going to do a certain thing. It is this: is or is not the amendment in order? Any argument which the Minister of Finance may have as to the desirability of doing a certain thing has nothing to do with the point of order before the chair. I would refer particularly to citation 551 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, which states:
551. It is a fundamental principle that no resolution or amendment to increase a charge upon the people can be moved with the Speaker in the chair; it must be initiated in committee by a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
All that has been done. Then, citation 553 states:
553. When it appeared from the debate that an amendment proposed to a resolution reported

from the committee of ways and means would increase the charge, the Speaker ruled the amendment out of order.
There is no attempt in this case to increase the charge or to reduce it in any way. Then, citation 555 reads:
555. No increase can be considered either of an existing, or of a new or temporary tax for the service of the year, except on the initiative of a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
I submit for your consideration that the question is not whether the Minister of Finance considers it advisable to give back to or take away certain privileges from the Bank of Canada, but rather whether or not the amendment is in order, according to the rule. Any other argument is beside the point, I submit.

I gathered from him that all taxation is to be abolished, that it is wrong for governments to tax.

The minister asked me to define what I meant by "debt free money", and I told him. I went on to say:
Under our proposals, if at any time too much money was in circulation, it would be taken out of circulation, either by taxation or through the price discount factor. But this is the point we make: that that money would not be taken out for the purpose of providing revenue for the government. It would be taken out in order to avoid inflation.
I can see where the minister might have got a mistaken impression. I was speaking extemporaneously, and I should have used the word "additional". If I had used the words "additional revenue" he would not have jumped to that conclusion. I should be opposed at this time to the idea of abolishing all taxation. I make that statement for this reason. We recognize that at the present time we have poverty, due largely to two facts: maldistribution of wealth, and a total deficiency of purchasing power to distribute wealth. In order to cover the first point, evidently you must have taxation to bring about a fairer distribution. But taxation will not cure the other condition, and for that purpose you must have an issue of new money.

So far as social credit proposals are concerned, I will touch very lightly on the point as to how we would bring about that eauilibrium.
If effective demand were only ninety per cent of production, we would propose a ten per cent discount in operation to restore that balance, and if production were to fall off by five per cent the discount would be reduced by five per cent in order to restore the balance. On the other hand, if production were to fall off by fifteen per cent the ten per cent discount would disappear entirely, and you would have a discount in reverse, in other words, a five per cent sales tax. I think the minister would admit that that would be fair. Everybody in the country would contribute to the relief of that national calamity by standing his share of the loss.
At page 1528 of Hansard, the minister is reported as follows:
The assumption inherent in the thinking of so many, that the government can issue money and have it perform its function, and by and by, when it comes back to the Bank of Canada, it can be destroyed without hurting anyone, is all nonsense, because the last man who held that bill and paid it into the Bank of Canada would be entitled to one dollar's worth of value from the Bank of Canada for it.
I agree with that statement, and that in itself is the greatest condemnation of the present system. But our proposal is entirely different, because I simply suggest that it might be necessary to tax it back if there was too much money in circulation, that is if there was excess demand against production. And in the event of a major calamity, where production fell off, there might be a discount in reverse. Everybody would share in the loss, and that would be perfectly equitable.

I cannot- understand how there could be at a given time a compilation of statistics which could accurately reflect immediately the velocity of circulation, which as I say is much more important in practice than its gross volume. Even if we had arrived at statistical perfection, which my hon. friends assume first of all, I cannot see how in the world the velocity factor would be reflected, which is really what millions of people are themselves doing with the currency they hold. Given the most perfect statistical machine, I do not see how you could get a sufficiently immediate appreciation of the velocity factor to be able to work out your elaborate just price, and discount and taxing-back provisions. The minister shakes his head. Some people may say this is just one of the haywire ideas of the Social Credit group, but I would point out that this is advocated by some leading economists and bankers to-day, and the number is steadily growing. I remember many years ago reading a book by Professor Soddy entitled Wealth, Virtual Wealth, and Debt, in which he advocated this very thing. Later I remember reading a book by Marshall Hattersley, who also advocated this scheme. A few years later I read a book by Professor Irving Fisher entitled One Hundred Per Cent Money, in which this same thing was advocated. Probably Professor Fisher is pne of the leading exponents of this proposal. Then I was much interested to receive a circular from Babsons, dated March 20, 1939, on the back of which appears a program for monetary reform; and I find that Babsons are now advocating the 100 per cent money system. So a person cannot just shrug his shoulders and disregard this proposal.

This new money (commission currency, or United States notes), would merely give an all cash backing for the cheeking deposits and medium of the country. A bank which previously had $100,000,000 of deposits subject to check with only $10,000,000 of cash behind them (along with $90,000,000 in securities) would send these $90,000,000 of securities to the currency commission in return for $90,000,000 more cash, thus bringing its total cash reserve up to $100,000,000 or 100 per cent of the deposits.
After this substitution of actual money for securities had been completed, the bank would be required to maintain permanently a cash reserve of 100 per cent against its demand deposits. In other words, the demand deposits would literally be deposits, consisting of cash held in trust for the depositor.
Thus, the new money would, in effect, be tied up by the 100 per cent reserve requirement.

speechtext: When the resolution preceding this bill was going through the house the other day, I recited the circumstances attendant upon the amendment a year ago of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Hon. members will remember that the Senate did not agree with the House of Commons on that occasion. Following the disagreement a conference was held under the rules governing such disagreements, and I do not think it is too much to say that the compromise finally agreed upon was not fully satisfactory to the House of Commons. In the interval we have had strong representations from the province of Manitoba-I believe I am correct in saying that the representations from the legislature of that province were unanimous-asking that the act be amended to place Manitoba in the same position as Saskatchewan and Alberta were placed in by the existing arrangement. This bill has as its object the complying with that request. For one, I sincerely trust that the other house will view the matter rather more favourably this year.

speechtext:
There was general disappointment following the action taken last year by the Senate with respect to the amendment proposed by this house to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. So far as the farmers are concerned, I do not think Manitoba is any better off than any other province in which the act still operates. Therefore, it was felt to be unjust and unfair that this act should be discontinued in this province. The legislature of the province of Manitoba was particularly interested in this matter from another angle. That province is attempting to meet a similar condition by what is termed a land court. I understand that representations have been made to this government to have legislation passed which will be necessary to make the provincial legislation effective. However, it is not thought that this object is possible
of accomplishment in the near future, and consequently there is a general desire to have this act continued until such time as the other legislation can be put into shape. I do not know the number of applications now before the board of review, which of course will be continued, but I do know that in going about the province one hears continuously the statement made that the act should be continued. I am satisfied that in the future there will be just as many cases to be dealt with as there have been in the past. So far as I am personally concerned, and I think the same can be said for other members from Manitoba, I am grateful that we are now being placed in the same position as the other prairie provinces with respect to this particular legislation. I trust this bill will meet with favourable consideration when it goes to the other house.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: RAILWAY SERVICES
subtopic: RATIFICATION OF CONVEYANCES OF CERTAIN LANDS TO TORONTO TERMINALS RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill is to clear some technical difficulties in connection with the title to the land now owned and used by the Toronto Terminal Railway Company. In 1904 a disastrous fire occurred in the locality

Railway Services-Toronto Terminals
of the former Grand Trunk station in Toronto. Following the fire the Grand Trunk Railway acquired certain land in the burnt area for extension of its terminal. In 1906 the Toronto Terminal Railway Company was formed to build the terminal, and the company entered into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, under the terms of which agreement the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific were to turn over such of their lands in the city of Toronto as the terminal company might require. The lands were duly turned over, and the terminal was built, as we all know; but although the railways have made every effort to satisfy the solicitors for the terminal company as to delivery of a clear title to the land occupied by the terminal, certain technical difficulties have made it impossible to do so.
One piece of land turned over by the Grand Trunk Railway was British ordnance land, and although a deed had been sent to Britain for execution, it now appears that the deed was never executed. In the meantime the British ordnance land had become Canadian ordnance land, and no proper deed of this property to the Grand Trunk Railway had ever been issued although the Grand Trunk had been enjoying uninterrupted possession of the land for some eighty years.
Similarly, part of the land to be conveyed by the Grand Trunk Railway is subject to an old undischarged mortgage of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The solicitors report that it is quite clear that under the terms of the settlement between the dominion government and the Grand Trunk Railway this land is the property of the Canadian National Railways, but in order to give clear title acceptable to the terminal company it is necessary for parliament to confirm the opinion of the railways that these mortgage rights have been extinguished.
I may add that in the event of the solicitors being mistaken and the former Grand Trunk shareholders having an equity in this land, which the solicitors feel sure they do not have, the bill provides for arbitration as between the Grand Trunk shareholders and the government through which the Grand Trunk shareholders may obtain from the courts any compensation that they can show is due them.
The third parcel of land is a matter between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Toronto Terminal Company. In the title of the land turned over by the Canadian Pacific Railway there is a flaw which is not particularly serious, but even though slight, it is considered desirable to clear the matter up as a part of this bill.
This bill was requested by the president of the Canadian National Railways and the
president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in a letter to myself signed by them jointly. The passage of this legislation will enable the Toronto Terminal Company to obtain a clear title to this property and to disburse certain moneys that are due the two railway companies on account of land which the}' turned over for the terminal project.

maintopic: RAILWAY SERVICES
subtopic: RATIFICATION OF CONVEYANCES OF CERTAIN LANDS TO TORONTO TERMINALS RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Might I ask the minister if there is any land involved in this other than what was ordnance land or land owned by the company? The point I have in mind is the question of jurisdiction dealing with property and civil rights, and such is entirely within the jurisdiction of a province unless the land has been vested in, we will say, the crown in the right of the dominion, or possibly in the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian National Railways, in which event I am not sure that provincial legislation will be required to deal with the land of either of those corporations or with ordnance lands. Has consideration been given to the necessity of getting provincial legislation in the same sense as the dominion legislation, because of the fact that we are dealing with property within a province, land which is within the jurisdiction of a province? I am inclined to think, if we were dealing only with ordnance lands or land that was vested in either of the two railway companies I have mentioned, that point might not arise. Is there any other land than land which was, at the time the transfers were made, under the control of, or vested in, or supposed to be vested in, either of these two companies? If we are seeking to vest land the title to which remains in some private individual or some corporation other than these two, I think there may be some question for consideration.

maintopic: RAILWAY SERVICES
subtopic: RATIFICATION OF CONVEYANCES OF CERTAIN LANDS TO TORONTO TERMINALS RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: There are three parcels of land involved. The second is land which was owned for many years by the Grand Trunk Railway but was subject to an undischarged mortgage of a junior security. The settlement between the Grand Trunk and the government, in the opinion of solicitors, vested that land in the crown.

subtopic: RATIFICATION OF CONVEYANCES OF CERTAIN LANDS TO TORONTO TERMINALS RAILWAY COMPANY

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. S. Woodsworth (Winnipeg North Centre) for the second reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the criminal code.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill under consideration at the present time would, if enacted, make it an offence for an employer to dismiss an employee merely because that employee belonged to a trade union. Brantford has many distinctions, among them being the fact that it is one of the most highly industrialized cities in the Dominion of Canada. I shall not take up the time of this house by enumerating the many and varied industries of that city, but with so many manufacturing concerns it is natural that our population should be made up to a very large extent of working people employed in these factories. They are the finest people in the world. The so-called working class of Brantford are industrious, law-abiding, patriotic, home-loving citizens. They are neither greedy nor grasping, but on the contrary are generous and fair-minded. To a great extent the same may be said of the employers of labour in that city, and as a result there have been very few strikes, lockouts or other labour troubles in
26S2

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
our fair city. Cooperation and a spirit of tolerance prevail among both employees and employers, with resulting harmony, peace and goodwill.
The working men and women have their own organizations. Some belong to trade unions; some belong to local associations, often organized among and limited to the employees of a particular factory. These organizations, I am reliably informed, are not only approved but in many instances encouraged by the employers. The workers committee acts as a connecting link between the workers and the management and interprets to each the viewpoint of the other. To my mind these labour organizations are doing a splendid service and should be encouraged, and this house should be eager to adopt any legislation which will improve their efficiency and do away with any discrimination.
I have given careful study and consideration to this bill, and I can say that it has my whole-hearted support. I was delighted to hear the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) state this afternoon that he is introducing an amendment to the criminal code to make effective the legislation proposed in this bill, the purpose of which is clearly set out in the explanatory note. As I stated in opening my remarks, this legislation, if enacted, will prevent employers from refusing to employ or from dismissing employees, or from conspiring with others therefor, for the reason that the employees are members of a trade union. The explanatory note adds:
As it is lawful for workmen or employees to form themselves into trade unions and to bargain collectively, it should, as a matter of public policy, be unlawful for employers to seek by overt acts or intimidation, threats or conspiracy to prevent them from belonging to such trade unions.
Two questions are involved in this bill. The first is the matter of the principle of the bill. Do we approve or disapprove the principle it sets out? The second question is one of jurisdiction. In other words, the whole matter might be summarized in this way: Should we approve the principle of the bill and, if we do, is it possible for us to deal with the matter under the jurisdiction granted to us under the terms of heading No. 27 of section 91 of the British North America Act? I will try, first, to show that the principle involved is sound and, second, that it is within our competence to deal with this legislation; and I may add as a corollary that even if there is a doubt, the act should be placed upon the statute TMr. W. R. Macdonald.]
books in order that it might be referred to the courts so that its validity might be determined.
This legislation was first introduced into the house in 1936. At that time it was not opposition to the principle of the bill that prevented its adoption; it did not pass because it was introduced so late in the session. Last year the bill was introduced again as Bill No. 4, and the opposition to it developed on constitutional grounds rather than otherwise. As a matter of fact, there seems to be little objection, either within or without the house, to the principle of the bill. A labour union, as everyone knows, is a permanent institution of men organized for their own protection and for the betterment of conditions of their contract of work. These unions have been recognized by both federal and provincial law. I * believe it is important that this point should be recognized before any privileges or rights are claimed for them. The federal Trade Unions Act defines "trade union" to mean:
-such combination, whether temporary or permanent, for regulating the relations between workmen and masters, or for imposing restrictive conditions on the conduct of any trade or business, as would, but for this act, have been deemed to be an unlawful combination by reason of some one or more of its purposes being in restraint of trade.
The Trade Unions Act itself is very careful not to invade provincial jurisdiction in regard to agreements and other matters. For instance, section 3 of the Trade Unions Act states in part as follows:
This act shall not affect
(b) any agreement between an employer and those employed by him as to such employment.
There is no doubt that such agreements do not fall within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament but come under the heading of property and civil rights under section 92 of the British North America Act. There is no inclination or desire to encroach in any way upon provincial rights. On the other hand, there also exist in the provinces trade and labour union acts which deal more extensively with the same subject, and there never has been any difficulty as to the extent of jurisdiction in civil matters. Further, the provincial laws provide for collective agreements and contracts respecting working conditions entered into between representatives of labour unions and representatives of employers or an employer himself. In addition, the provincial authorities may generally order that any such collective labour agreements respecting any trade or industry shall also bind all employees and employers in a stated region within the

26S3
Criminal Code-Trade Unions
province, that is, if it does not interfere with federal legislation such as the Conciliation and Labour Act.
Now, to continue with the rights of members of trade unions which are recognized by law, it is admitted that they have the right to strike, just as much as employers have the right of lockout. In the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act "strike" is defined as follows:
"Strike" or "to go on strike," without limiting the nature of its meaning, means the cessation.of work by a body of employees acting in combination, or a concerted refusal or a refusal under a common understanding of any number of employees to continue to work for an employer, in consequence of a dispute, done as a means of compelling their employer, or to aid other employees in compelling their employer, to accept terms of employment.
The word "dispute" is defined as:
. . . any difference between an employer and one or more of his employees, as to matters or things affecting or relating to work done or to be done by him or them, or as to the privileges, rights and duties of employers or employees, not involving any such violation thereof as constitutes an indictable offence. . . .
And so on. Certain strikes have been declared to be illegal by our criminal code. If there is anything that interferes with contracts, property or civil rights, above all things it is a strike. Nevertheless the criminal code by section 590 states:
No prosecution shall be maintainable against any person for conspiracy in refusing to work with or for any employer or workman, or for doing any act or causing any act to be done for the purpose of a trade combination, unless such act is an offence punishable by statute.
Section 499 of the code provides for a certain number of cases where it is an offence punishable on indictment or on summary conviction to go on strike, if thereby one wilfully breaks a contract, with danger to life or property, or a contract connected with a supply of power, light,, gas or water, or relating to the mails, and so on.
I do not think it is necessary to insist any further on this point, because there is no doubt that both provincially and federally labour has the right to organize itself as labour or trade unions, and to act as such within certain limits prescribed by law. Although they have the right to organize as labour unions, the criminal code makes it a crime for them to go beyond certain limits. For instance, although men may strike, they would not have the right, in so doing, to intimidate other people, to use violence, to follow people from place to place, to deprive others of the use of their tools, or to beset or watch the houses of others.
The purpose of the bill is that the criminal code should deal with employers in the same manner as it deals with employees. The law has given certain rights. These rights have been limited on the one hand, but if they are to exist at all they should be guaranteed and protected. If employees on strike are not permitted to use violence or to intimidate co-workers or their employers, I submit that employers should not be permitted to seek by intimidation, threat of loss of employment, to prevent men from doing what they have a perfect right to do-which is all that is asked by this bill.
This brings us to the constitutional aspect of the question. I do not intend to deal at length with this point, because I am quite willing to admit that the constitutional right of parliament to enact such legislation has been put in doubt iby some of the constitutional authorities in this house. On the other hand, I am sure that we could find in the house just as great a number of lawyers who would be willing to argue as to the constitutionality of section 502A as proposed to be inserted in the code iby section 1 of the bill.
I am conversant with the decisions of the privy council and of our supreme court with respect to the restricted power of this parliament as to the creation of new crimes. For instance, in the judgment in The Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider and the Attorneys-General of Canada and of Ontario, delivered by Viscount Haldane on January 20, 1925, the learned lord referred to the decision of the board wherein has been laid down the interpretation of section 91, head 27, of the British North America Act. He recalled that in the Reciprocal Insurers case, Mr. Justice Duff, of our own court, stated definitely the true interpretation in delivering the judgment of the judicial committee where, summing up' the effect of the series of previous decisions relating to the point, he said:
In accordance with the principle inherent in these decisions their lordships think it is no longer open to dispute that the parliament of Canada cannot, by purporting to create penal sanctions under section 91, head 27, appropriate to itself exclusively a field of jurisdiction in which, apart from such a procedure, it could exert no legal authority, and that if, when examined as a whole, legislation in form criminal is found, in aspects and for purposes exclusively within the provincial sphere, to deal with matters committed to the provinces, it cannot be upheld as valid.
In the earlier Board of Commerce case (1922, Appeal Cases 191) the principle to be applied was laid down in the same way. It was pointed out that the dominion had exclusive legislative power to create new crimes "*where the subject matter is one which, by its very nature, belongs to the domain of

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
criminal jurisprudence." But "it is quite another thing, first to attempt to interfere with a class of subject committed exclusively to the provincial legislature, and then to justify this by enacting ancillary provisions, designated as new phrases of dominion criminal law, which require a title to so interfere as the basis of their application."
On the other hand, in the recent reference to the privy council with respect to section 498A of the criminal code, their lordships said:
The only limitation on the plenary power of the dominion to determine what shall or shall not be criminal is the condition that parliament shall not, in the guise of enacting criminal legislation in truth and in substance, encroach on any of the classes of subjects enumerated in section 92. It is no objection that it does in fact affect them. In a genuine attempt to amend the criminal law it may obviously affect previous existing civil rights.
And further:
In the present case there seems to be no reason for supposing that the dominion is using the criminal law as a pretence or pretext or that the legislation is in pith and substance in any way interfering with civil rights in the province.
Let us for a minute turn our attention to section 498A of the criminal code. What does it state? It says:
Every person engaged in trade or commerce or industry is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty who is a party to any transaction of sale which discriminates against competitors of the purchaser in that any discount, rebate or allowance is granted to the purchaser over and above any discount, rebate or allowance available at the time of such transaction to the competitors in respect of a sale of goods of like quality and quantity.
Surely if that is not interfering with contracts and freedom of contract and if it is not, according to the privy council, an invasion of civil rights, could not the same be said of an amendment the purpose of which is to prevent employers from seeking by overt acts, intimidation, threats or conspiracy, to prevent free men from doing what they have a perfect right to do? I submit that there is nothing wrong in se in granting to one purchaser a lower price than is granted to another prospective purchaser. On the other hand, it is wrong in se to threaten or to intimidate the same person when he is acting within his rights. If it is possible under the criminal code to create a crime and an offence out of the first act, then there is ten times as much justification for doing so in the second case. It is one thing to interfere with civil rights, such as the right to contract, and thus invade provincial legislation, but this proposed legislation does not invade the right of free contract and civil rights within the province. On the contrary, we are confirming that right 
when we make it a crime for anyone to prevent these same rights from being properly exercised.
It is my civil right to join a labour association. If anyone should seek by intimidation or threat to prevent me from exercising such a right there could be no doubt that this would be an offence, because the person doing so would be interfering with the liberty of the subject, one of the great rights granted in 1215 to Anglo-Saxon people by the Magna Charta, from which all our rights are derived. This cannot be said to be legislation in form criminal for purposes exclusively within the provincial sphere. I submit respectfully that this bill does not deal in any way with the matters committed to the provinces. As stated in the Board of Commerce case in 1922, the dominion has exclusive legislative power to create new crimes where the subject matter is one which by its very nature belongs in the domain of criminal jurisprudence. Certainly this is what is being done by this bill. There is no attempt to interfere in any way with that class of subject committed exclusively to the provincial legislatures. Any reasoning by which their lordships were able to uphold the validity of section 498A of the criminal code applies with even greater force with respect to the validity of the section which it is proposed by this bill to insert in the criminal code.
I should like to conclude by repeating the practical suggestion which was made last year by the then leader of the opposition, the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett, and which was quoted some time ago in this house by the hon. member for Winnipeg' North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). The Right Hon. Mr. Bennett said:
If we have the strongest reason in the world for believing a statute to be valid, we should place it on the statute books and ask that it be referred to the court so that its validity may be determined. That is the method prescribed by law for that purpose.
I feel that the principle of this bill should be endorsed by this house, either in its present form or in the form in which the right hon. the Minister of Justice proposes to deal with the matter. For the reasons stated, I shall support the bill.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak for more than a few minutes. First, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) upon the fair way in which he dealt with the subject matter of this bill and upon his excellent presentation. About thirty-five years ago I was a member of a trade union, and I continued my membership for some years. The company with which I was connected at that time employed between three and four thousand men, and they were insistent that their employees should be trade unionists. As I remember, they would not engage a man who was not a member of a trade union. Their experience was that the trade unionist was a thoroughly trained man, whether he was a machinist or a member of any other craft. The company realized that if they engaged trade unionists they would be certain of having capable and competent employees.
I am surprised to learn that to-day there are apparently employers who refuse to employ trade unionists or who dismiss men because they are members of a union. Certainly this should not be allowed. I am certain, however, that the vast majority of employers are more partial to trade unionists than they are to those who are not members of such unions. I am not referring to the employer who employs only a small number of men because I am not so familiar with that phase of industry. I do know, however, that the large employers realize that most of the improvements which have been brought about in working conditions, most of the increased efficiency in their plants and the freedom of their employees from injury, are the result of what the trade unions have done. The system of inspecting plants in order to ascertain that machines are properly guarded to prevent the loss of fingers or hands was instigated by the trade unions. Some years ago the health of workmen was endangered by dust or fumes of one kind or another, but all this has been changed. To-day in well regulated plants there is no possibility of injury to health from these causes. All these improvements have been brought about by the efforts of earnest men who were at the head of our trade unions. They have beseeched and urged employers to improve working conditions and provide safeguards. Where they were not successful, they were able to persuade their representatives in parliament to enact laws to that end.
I am in accord with the principle of this bill. I certainly would be opposed to the
dismissal of an employee or the non-employment of a worker because he happened to belong to a trade union. I cannot comprehend any large plant working against their own interests by such intimidations or threats. I cannot understand such a large organization working against the interests of its workers by doing the things referred to in this bill. My experience has been-and I have been associated not recently but some years ago with large numbers of workers- that anything that was done for the benefit of the worker in the plant resulted in more production, which was of great benefit to the firm itself. I have always felt that and do to-day, so that with the general principle of this bill I am glad to say I am in happy accord.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
In any event the principle of the bill is apparently going to be covered by an amendment to be brought in by the minister. The reason I was struck, when the bill was introduced, with the necessity of saying a few words in support of it was that I was shocked to think that in any large way

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
at all such a thing as this bill seeks to prevent should take place in Canada. I cannot imagine that it often happens in this dominion that an employer of labour would consider dismissing an employee because he belonged to a trade union. After all, unionization has been recognized for the last seventy years or thereabouts. It is true that prior to that time in England unionization was not permitted as it is to-day. Indeed, it was a crime even in that very far advanced nation, to advocate the unionization of employees. One of the great advantages which democracies have over dictatorships is that we have this freedom of association and the right to collective bargaining and the unionization of workers which do not exist to-day in countries like Germany, Italy and Russia. The right of workers to organize, associate together and bargain collectively which the democracies still possess is an advantage over anything of which the dictator countries can boast.
I do not need to take up any more of the time of the house. It is sufficient to say that I am entirely in sympathy with the principle of this bill, and having listened to the debate and heard the views of various speakers from different sections of the house, I imagine that the minister will not introduce this session a measure that will be more unanimously approved than the amendment he proposes to bring in to the criminal code to cover this bill.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) this evening, I do not know whether it is necessary to say anything further on this bill. The minister may think some of us in this group are rather a bad lot, but I wish to let him know that, long before I ever came into this house, I had come to regard him with a great deal of esteem, and that was largely because of the reports I heard of him from the hon. member for AVinnipeg North Centre (Mr. AVoodsworth), who is not in his seat this evening. I am sure that the hon. member for AVinnipeg North Centre will be greatly pleased that the minister has seen his way clear to bringing in a measure to give effect to the principle that the hon. member has been advocating for so long, and I trust that the bill will meet all the requirements.
There is one matter on which I should like to say a word, a matter on which I have had a great many communications, so that I desire to put some of them on record. AVe have had in British Columbia at all events-and I have no doubt it is the same in some of the other provinces-what is called a black list; that is,
TMr. Manion.l
workers would be dismissed, by one employer for trade union activities, and then other employers would be notified, so that it became quite impossible for these workers to get employment. I remember that this matter was brought to the attention of the house in 1935 by the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) who gave what I think was a very fair illustration of how the black list worked in British Columbia. Since Bill No. 5 was introduced, I have received quite a number of communications in regard to the operation of the black list, and all these complaints are accompanied by affidavits. I shall take the time to read one only, but it is typical of all the others. This is an affidavit that was made by Charles Kingsley. It reads:
I, Charles Kingsley, of the AVest Hotel, 444 Carrall street, in the city of Vancouver, in the province of British Columbia, make oath and say as follows:
1.	I have read the annexed statement which is signed by myself, and the same is true and accurate in every respect.
2.	I am the Charles Kingsley therein mentioned.
This affidavit was sworn before a notary public in and for the province of British Columbia. The statement of Charles Kingsley reads as follows:
I have worked in the woods in British Columbia since 1920 as a logger and have never been discharged for inefficiency or other cause except as mentioned below.
Between February and May 1934 I was active in the loggers' strike being in charge of the union relief for married strikers.
Following the strike I went back to work in Camp 4 of the Alberni Pacific Lumber Company, and remained on the job for a period of about four weeks. At that time approximately one hundred (100) men, all members of the union, were laid off. including myself. No reason was given for this lay-off but the camp continued operating with other employees. I am therefore of the opinion that the lay-off was directed against the union.
Since that time I have filled out the required application form at the loggers' agency (commonly known as Black's agency)-
By the way, that name .Black's Agency, indicates how this form of discrimination has come to be known in British Columbia as the black list.
Mr. MAYHEAAL AVould the hon. member mind telling me the date of the affidavit?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to. It says:
Sworn before me at the city of Vancouver, B.C., this 31st day of January, 1939.
The statement continues:
Since that time I have filled out the required application form at the loggers' agency (commonly known as Black's agency), 876 Hornby street, but although my application has been

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
on file for nearly five years I have not secured a job through the said agency. I have had many interviews with the agency and have never been able to secure from it other than vague statements as to the reason for my being unable to secure employment and I firmly believe that because of my union activity I am a victim of the "black-list system," particularly as I never had trouble in securing work before the 1934 strike.
In order to attempt to secure a position for myself, I have written to Hon. G. S. Pearson, Minister of Labour, on July 13, 1936, and February 28, 1938, calling attention to the situation above outlined, and asking for help. The replies which the minister sent me are attached to and form a part of this statement, and from his letter dated February 24, 1938, I gather that he too regards my employment through any agency of the loggers' association an impossibility, since he advised me to get work with some logging company outside the said association.
Then there are the letters from George S. Pearson, minister of labour of British Columbia.
Charles Kingsley, Esquire,
% West hotel, 440 Carrall street,
Vancouver, B.C.
Victoria, July 30, 1936.
Dear Sir:
I have received a reply from the B.C. Loggers' Association secretary and he states they have absolutely nothing against you, but that there has been a very great surplus of labour in the class in which you work and on this account they have not been able to offer you a position. However, he intimates that if you apply further they will try to find something for you as soon as possible. My suggestion is that you again make application to the loggers' association agency.
Yours very truly,
Geo. S. Pearson,
Minister.
In a later letter, dated February 24, 1938, writing to Mr. Kingsley again Mr. Pearson said:
Dear Sir:
I have your letter dated February 28th in which you complain of your inability to get work through the loggers' association.
It is rather difficult for me to help you in this matter as I cannot dictate to employers as to whom they should employ.
I understand, however, that the loggers' association employs less than half of the loggers that are employed in British Columbia, and that there are two other agencies who act for other logging companies.
I would suggest that you go down to the employment service of Canada and have a talk with Mr. Mitchell or Mr. McVety and see if they can help you in getting work with some logging company outside of the association.
Yours very truly,
Geo. S. Pearson,
Minister.
That affidavit, which is only.one of many that I have received, gives a fairly clear indication, I believe, of how the black list operates
in British Columbia. Last year, when I spoke in support of a bill similar to this one, I said that I was in favour of the recognition of trades unions, that I felt that proper recognition of trades unions by employers was not only necessary for the smooth operation of industry, but also necessary if there is to be any reality to what we call our democratic system of government. We cannot educate people, open up their minds and quicken their intelligences, and then expect that they are going to be satisfied to be treated like cattle in the positions which they occupy in industry. Because they are men they will insist upon asserting their rights in taking some part in the direction of the industries in which they work. I have in mind a statement made by Mr. Justice McIntosh, whom the government of British Columbia have had occasion to call in during the past few years in connection with a number of labour disputes. I believe I mentioned last year that, in his report on the dispute between the Burns Packing company and its employees, he stated that he felt satisfied the trouble would never have started if the company had been accustomed to dealing with their employees as trade unionists, and if the union officials had been experienced representatives. A great deal of the difficulty which developed, he said, was due to the lack of experience of the management in dealing with their employees on a trades union basis, and so far as the employees were concerned, to a lack of appreciation of their responsibility which goes with a properly organized trade union. The loggers' union of British Columbia can supply any number of instances of the operation of the black list in that province.
In closing, I wish to commend the Minister of Justice for the step he has taken in this very important matter.

speechtext:
I wish to congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) upon having seen his way clear to take up this bill and make a government measure of it. Unquestionably, organized labour in Canada has contributed a very great deal to the economic life of our country, and it has rendered good service on a number of occasions when intimidation has been used against men for being members of a labour organization. I have belonged to organized labour all my working days, but fortunately I have belonged to one of the railroad brotherhoods, and we have been dealing with men who for a good many years have been doing business with organized labour and appreciate what it means to be able to make contracts so that they will know

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
what their expenses on operations are going to be for a considerable time in advance. I do not propose to take up any more time; I just wanted to state that I am in entire accord with this bill, because I feel it is going to fill a need which has been long felt in this country.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
I would not delay the passage of this bill; rather I would do everything in my power to push it along; so what I have to say will take only a moment.
The principle of the bill is sound. I am glad to see that there is such unanimity of expression in its favour from many speakers in the house. We owe to trades unionism in this country much that is of value for the security of our working men. There has always been a question in my mind regarding the criminality of the act under one clause in particular. That clause, I see, has been changed somewhat, and perhaps it may be further changed when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) brings in the government bill. Nevertheless I realize that heavy fines may not achieve the purpose for which this bill is created, and if infraction of the act must be made a criminal offence in order to put teeth into the law I am quite in favour of it.
As regards the black-list tactics which were mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), some time ago I made inquiries in the city of Hamilton, and I found that employers of labour, far from being anxious to make use of the black list, were anxious to treat with the trades unions and do everything possible to keep satisfied workmen in their plants.
I am heartily in accord with the bill and I shall certainly support it.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: I want to take this opportunity of adding my support to the bill and expressing my agreement with the attitude of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). Having the honour to represent the constituency of Welland, in which there is a great diversification of industry, including almost every kind of occupation, I find that generally this bill meets with the approval of labour in my riding. Therefore I am pleased to support the bill. I concur in the remarks made by the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald), and I am also in accord with the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), which seem to me very much to the point.

I am pleased indeed at the unanimity with which the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth)

has been supported. It shows the advance that this house is making in connection with matters affecting trade unions. I was more than pleased to hear the announcement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) this afternoon when he said he would incorporate in the criminal code the principle of the bill. In view of that fact, it would be almost out of place for me this evening to discuss this bill I would far sooner speak to the question when the Minister of Justice brings in his amendments to the criminal code. speechtext: As the explanatory note indicates, this is the operating provision of the act. The necessity for this section arises more particularly from the prospective visit of His Majesty the King. During his majesty's presence in Canada, it would not be possible, under existing laws and practice, to issue royal instruments in relation to Canadian matters under the great seal or the signet of the United Kingdom. His majesty may be called upon to issue such instruments during the period of his visit in Canada-that is, for Canadian matters-and section 8 makes provision for the passing of such instruments under the great seal of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ISSUE OP BOYAL INSTRUMENTS AND ORDERS AND REGULATIONS WITH RESPECT THEREOF
speechtext:
Section
l is to enable permanent provision to be made for subjecting Canadian transactions involving the use of the royal seal, in form as well as in substance, to the direct control and responsibility of Canadian ministers. As it is to-day, shere is no statute governing the matter; it is under convention. When the use of the

Royal Seals
royal seal is necessitated on instruments, treaties, for instance, it is done on the recommendation of a Secretary of State in the United Kingdom, but at the request of a dominion minister, and it is usually countersigned by a responsible Canadian minister. But it is not done under statute; it is merely convention. This will have the effect of making the substance and the form agree. It may be done in the same way but under order in council of Canada, always subject to the approval of His Majesty the King. This is merely enabling legislation to make the present situation agree with the constitutional development of Canada.
