Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and
Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 81, to provide for the supervision and regulation of trading in grain futures.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I desire to make a few observations in connection with this measure, which I would say has been badly needed for many years in western Canada. Some control over the operations of the Winnipeg clearing house and the Winnipeg grain exchange is absolutely necessary. I believe if this legislation had been in force last fall, even in its present form, it would have saved this government and the people of Canada many millions of dollars; for, if I am correctly informed, certain large selling operations by the big international firms took place on the exchange shortly after the announcement of the government's policy with respect to the eighty cent fixed price and the selling of grain, which had a depressing effect on the market. Had a supervisor been in charge, I think there is no doubt that he would have prohibited much of the selling that took place. I believe it is agreed by all concerned that during the last twenty-five years the free and uncontrolled operation of the Winnipeg grain exchange has cost the producers of western Canada many millions of
Grain Futures-Mr. Perley

dollars. In my opinion it is doubtful if the exchange would 'be necessary at all if we had a proper wheat board and a board using the powers granted to it.
I am not going to take very long, but for a few moments I should like to examine some of the evidence heard by the Turgeon commission, since this bill is based upon a recommendation contained in the report of that commission. I have devoted quite a considerable time to the study and review of some of that evidence. Perhaps not very many members of this house realize that the evidence given before that commission covers some fourteen or fifteen thousand pages. The report deals with some of the evidence, but it is an almost impossible task to make a careful study of all the evidence presented, as I am sure all hon. members will appreciate. However, I have gone through the index of the evidence and made some notes in regard to points that I think are of importance.
The commission went overseas and heard the evidence of some buyers in regard to what they thought would happen if the Winnipeg futures market were closed, and I should like to give a few quotations in that regard. A number of witnesses were asked by the commissioner and the counsel who accompanied him overseas what if any difficulty they would anticipate to the producers of western Canada if the Winnipeg futures market were closed. At page 10372, David Muir, of Glasgow, manager of the Scottish Cooperative Wholesale Society, said he saw no difficulty if the Winnipeg futures market were closed. Mr. Bracey, buyer for the English C.W.S., which is also a wholesale society of Liverpool, at page 10492 said the advantage would be all to the producer if the Winnipeg market were closed. At page 10446 Mr. Snodgrass, a Glasgow miller, said:
If it disappeared (that is, the Winnipeg market) I would not like to say that we could not get on quite well without it.
The evidence of some of the members of the Glasgow Corn Association was taken. At page 10392 one of them said that if the Winnipeg futures market were closed there would be one less market to watch. I do not think it necessary to take the time to quote many of the additional, similar statements that were made; that is the evidence of overseas buyers as to what they thought would be the result if the market were closed.
I should like now to give the house some information in regard to the extent to which overseas buyers use the Winnipeg market for hedging purposes. I find that the general consensus of opinion expressed in the evidence given by millers and merchants in the

countries visited by the commission was that they used the Winnipeg market for hedging purposes only occasionally. One witness said that apart from the three big English millers practically no hedging at all was done by the United Kingdom miller. Then on the continent Alphonse Van Kan, president of the Belgian Millers' Association, at page 10684 said that speaking as a miller he hedged very little. Another gentleman, Mr. Van Lompa, a Belgian miller, at page 10703 said:
We have never used the option market in respect to a single bushel in our existence.
Those are buyers and millers on the continent and in the United Kingdom. Then at page 10496 a man by the name of McFayden, connected with the Scottish wholesale society of Liverpool, said he could not see the necessity at all for dealing in options on the Winnipeg market. We have another by Mr. Stuych, broker at Antwerp who, at page 10778 of the evidence said he seldom hedges when he buys, depending upon his view of the market. Then, Pillman of the British National Millers' Association states at page 9682 that his firm never had to hedge in fifty years of operation. Another man, Jordan, a French miller, states that he neither buys nor sells on the Winnipeg futures market.
These are a few quotations I have compiled from the evidence, and I give them here just to show that so far as the Winnipeg futures market is concerned the evidence is conclusive that it would not adversely affect the producer in western Canada, if it were closed, and also to show that the buyers that we are depending on in Great Britain and Europe do not use it for hedging, to any great amount.
Let me give the house briefly some idea of the volume of trading, and then I want hon. members to ask themselves if they think it is necessary. I might mention that the compilation of this information was a heavy task. When I visited the sessional papers office and took occasion to go through some of the evidence, I asked the man in charge how many hon. members had been in his office and had asked to see and to review the evidence. He said there had been only three, and he named the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, a Liberal member from Saskatchewan and myself. He said the Liberal member looked at the volume of stuff, turned over a few pages and said, "Well, this is quite a job." Then, on turning over some more pages, he made the further remark, "I do not think it would be parliamentary"-and that was the only time he visited the office or interested himself in the matter. I might say further the

Grain Futures-Mr. Perley
leader of the opposition also looked it over and discussed it. He realized what a task it would be to get anything out of it, and made only one visit to the office.
I was more interested, and I have compiled a few notes. Part of the evidence made reference to the commission headed by Sir Josiah Stamp. At page 49 of the evidence before that commission there was reference to the volume of trading on the Winnipeg market. They took the year 1929 as a normal crop year. The crop in that year was 304,000,000 bushels. First, may I point out there was evidence to the effect that buying and selling hedges on the Winnipeg market are seldom equal; in fact, they are far from being equal.
Evidence was given as to the records of Mr. McFarland's trading in one year. There were records of the pools' trading, and those records showed that of the 184,000,000 bushels traded in, 175,000,000 were buying hedges by McFarland, or under his operations. So that the selling hedges, making up the balance, were out of proportion to the buying hedges.
I .now come to the volume of trading in 1929. I would recall to the minds of hon. members that 1929 was a year when there was practically a collapse in our markets. There was a collapse in the markets of the world, so far as the sale of our wheat was concerned. That was the year when the pools were in difficulties. Records show that of the wheat taken over by McFarland when he undertook operations of stabilization in which he undertook to sell the surplus wheat then accumulated, forty-seven per cent was held by the grain trade and fifty-three per cent by the pools. That year has been taken as an average, however, and, as I pointed out before, that was a year in which prices practically collapsed.
The point I wish to make is that when the grain exchange was in full operation, it could not take care of the situation and did not function properly. We take the year 1929 with its crop of 304.000,000 bushels. The average traded on the Winnipeg grain exchange from May 1, 1929, to March 31, 1931, was 23,488,000 bushels daily. The highest trading in one day was 38,000.000 bushels, and over the whole period the average was 24,000,000 bushels daily. In 1929 there were 300 trading days. The total traded in, bought and sold, amounted to 7,200,000,000 bushels, made up as I shall describe. Of the crop of 304,000,000 bushels the pool handled, unhedged, 121,000,000 bushels. The amount retained for seed and feed was 50,000,000 bushels. I think that was a little short. The hedgeable grain stood at 133.000,000 bushels. The carryover of the pools'
share of the crop, unhedged, was 91,000,000 bushels, and the hedgeable carryover in the grain trade was 48,000,000 bushels, leaving a total of 43,000,000 bushels of the carryover to be hedged. Or, in other words, there was a total of 176,000,000 bushels of cash grain actually to go through the exchanges on the open market, and to be hedged.
As I said a moment ago, the volume of trading was 7,200,000,000 bushels; in other words, they bought and sold the crop forty-one times. The point I wish to make is this: Does anyone think it is necessary to permit an organization to proceed in that way, especially when in the year they did that amount of trading there was a collapse in the markets and there was no effort on their part to keep the price up? Do hon. members think it is necessary that we permit such an organization to carry on?
I should like now to review the report of Mr. Justice Turgeon, and to point out a few advantages I believe a Canadian wheat board operating exclusively might have. I would not say they would have 100 per cent control; but if with the assistance of the bill we are now considering there were a tightening up on the market, and the board were properly functioning, they would be almost in control to operate 100 per cent. They would always hold prices at competitive values. It could instantly meet price cutting. It could tend to reduce fluctuation in prices. It could negotiate with foreign semi-governmental bodies where centralized buying and quota restrictions are now to be found. It could best handle things in an emergency. This is evidenced by the report of the Turgeon commission. Such a board could assist in the development of a national agricultural policy. I believe this government is making some little effort toward that end. The board could protect the producers of western Canada. These producers generally are satisfied with the act, and if the board were properly operating, they would also be satisfied with it. The board could do one more important thing. It could be a real competitor to the large international firms which are now working on the exchange and which have much greater control than many of us realize. I am informed that last fall the "big three" played a very important part in the selling operations which depressed the price.
Mr. Justice Turgeon reported that the board was the only system which could function properly in an emergency. It was stated in the report that the open market cannot function properly in an emergency. The commissioner has admitted in his report that the board is the only agency which is best adapted

Grain Futures-Mr. Perley
to act in an emergency. The commissioner admits that a government agency is best under the present haphazard method of negotiating with countries where centralized or partly centralized buying is in vogue. There is no argument against that. Evidence is given at page 9996 by Australian witnesses that international agreements might be necessary within the next five years. I think we shall have to have some international arrangement in connection with the marketing if we continue to produce as we have produced, and the Australians think that will come within the next five years.
Mr. Abrahams, an old country buyer, stated at page 10576 that the grain trade has changed completely in the various countries, that importation is not allowed in many countries except under special licence. He stated that in Italy and Germany there is no longer free trade in wheat, and that the trade in various countries is entirely in the hands of the governments. Mr. Smith of the Winnipeg grain exchange, who is also president of one of the large exporting companies, stated at page 3034 that they sell to government agencies. The same witness stated at page 3088 that the Italians bought wheat under government supervision only. Hon. members must remember that this is one of our principal Canadian exporters. He stated at page 3089 that Holland has a government agency in New York through which they have to operate. Here is the evidence that a government agency can deal more adequately with the situation.
I do not think there is any question that the Canadian Wheat Board Act must stand. More power should be given to the board to permit them to become exporters of wheat. In view of the evidence which we have had and the difficult period that is ahead of us-this is declared to be an emergency year-I think we should consider the question of a grain exchange or no grain exchange. That is something which it might be well for this parliament to consider. In the last twenty years or so we have had seventeen inquiries into the grain business. Many of them have not been of much value. There has been no inquiry into the operations of the exchange such as I should like to have. Hon. members will recall that back in 1936, when the Turgeon commission was set up, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and I made a plea to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) to see to it that the commission made a thorough inquiry into the operations of the grain exchange in Winnipeg. I have in my hand some of the correspondence which occurred following that request made in the

house. I have letters between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself, between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and Mr. Ralston who was counsel for the commission, between the minister and the commissioner and between the minister and Mr. Bennett. This correspondence goes to show that there was no intention of making an inquiry into the grain trade such as was made into the textile business.
This inquiry should not have been conducted by members of the legal fraternity; it should have been carried on by men selected by industry or from the busines world. Then we would not have had the legal battles which occurred many times during the sessions of this commission. I think the public is weary of royal commissions made up of a lot of legal talent and surrounded with a lot of legal red tape. I sat in on a few of the sessions of this commission, and on two or three occasions I heard the lawyers arguing as to whether questions were in order and so on. It was just a legal battle. I suggest that hon. members look at this report. On one page they will see a list of the counsel connected with this commission. There were some twenty or more lawyers connected in one way or another with this inquiry, although not all were on the government payroll. Had they all been paid at the rate at which one or two of them were, the inquiry would have cost us a fortune. Twenty-one lawyers representing different interests in western Canada followed the commission. We provided for the cost of this commission last year, but I think it would be interesting if we knew the total amount that had been paid in legal fees to the twenty odd lawyers who followed this commission across Canada.
I said at the outset of my remarks that I thought this bill was something which we should have had many years ago. To-day is practically the first time I have seen this bill.
I notice it provides for a supervisor, and apparently not too much power is to be given to him.
I would prefer if we had had a comptroller with the power to stop trading in futures at any moment. Apparently it is the intention of the minister to give that power to the supervisor, and I should like to see it made very plain that this supervisor will have sufficient authority to stop trading at any time, and certainly to prohibit selling such as we are led to believe went on last fall. I do not know whether the bill is to go to a committee, but I suggest that it should because it deals with a very important matter. This evening I have set out some of the facts which were disclosed in the evidence given before the

Grain Futures-Mr. Hay hurst
Turgeon commission, but there is much more information worthy of consideration to be found in this evidence which is now in the sessional papers office.
I appreciate the fact that a great many members of this house are not conversant with western conditions, and I hardly think one can get an intelligent decision on the merits of the bill in committee of the whole because it involves consideration of the intricacies of a complicated and very important institution. I would ask the minister just how far, for instance, he took into consideration the rules and regulations of the Chicago board of trade and the provisions of the Commodity Exchange Act by which the Chicago board of trade operates, and how far he is endeavouring in this measure to follow the rules and regulations governing trading by that organization. There is no doubt in my mind that if sufficient powers of control were given to the supervisor he could prevent the manipulation of corners and squeezes, as they are called. That is something which certainly should not be permitted, and could be prevented with proper control.
In conclusion, there are one or two suggestions I should like to make if the bill goes to a committee. I would ask the committee and the Minister of Trade and Commerce to give serious consideration to making the port of Vancouver and the port of Churchill points of delivery for all transactions implemented on the Winnipeg exchange. I think there is a strong discrimination being exercised against these two ports. The members from western Canada I think will agree with me that if we can do anything to facilitate the getting of business for the port of Churchill it is our business to do it. For certain months of the year that port should be made a point of delivery for all future contracts.
I do not wish to take further time in discussing the bill. I would suggest that the minister allow it to go to a committee, possibly the committee on agriculture, where some other important measures affecting western wheat growers and producers, such as trading in grain, and other matters are to be considered, because I think this bill could be more intelligently reviewed there. With all respect for the members of the house, very few but western members have any knowledge of what goes on in the institution for which it is now proposed to appoint a supervisor with powers of control. The very fact that it is considered necessary to appoint a supervisor for this clearing house is an evidence of its great importance, and I think the members from western Canada would be the ones best fitted to consider this measure in detail in a committee.
I have here the Commodity Exchange Act under which the Chicago board of trade is operating, and it is a very long and complicated act. I have already asked the minister how far he and his officers considered this act when drafting this bill. There are very many provisions in this act and rules and regulations governing trading on the Chicago board of trade that we should take into consideration. While I leave it to the best judgment of the minister, I do feel that this is one measure upon which we can profitably spend some little time and that we can consider it best in the committee on agriculture. We cannot give it the consideration it deserves in committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, listening to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), I thought probably I should say a few words on this bill. Most of the members from western Canada know that the people who lose money on the market are the very ones who can least afford to do so. From my own training I am perhaps in a position to speak on this question because my people have been millers for generations back in the old country. In the old land the Liverpool corn exchange and other corn exchanges are not used to the same extent as the Winnipeg grain exchange or the Chicago grain exchange for purposes of pure speculation or gambling. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle says that men bought futures and then were squeezed. I would call that unprincipled manipulation. I have observed rye being quoted in some years on the Winnipeg exchange at a higher price than wheat, and yet we all know that the intrinsic value of rye is not as high as that of wheat, but the price is sent up probably because of a corner in that commodity at that particular time.
From my experience I would say that we should have a 100 per cent wheat board, and I should like to read what the Turgeon commission said in that regard:
For all these reasons (and notwithstanding the adverse considerations to which I have referred in relation to government boards) I do not feel that I can suggest the immediate dissolution of the Canadian wheat board.
I understand another bill is coming in which will bring about a 100 per cent wheat board. The Turgeon report continues:
There is a strong possibility that conditions may develop which will require a measure of assistance in the marketing of the coming crop, and I do not know, of course, how long these conditions may continue after the final chapter of this report is written. In the meantime I can think of nothing better to suggest than that the board be maintained to meet any situation which may arise.
2G94

Grain Futures-Mr. Hay hurst
As I said in my opening remarks, the people who lose money trading on the exchange are the ones who can ill afford to lose it. Why do they lose money? Because gambling has an appeal and it is perhaps the spirit of sportsmanship within us all that tempts people to' take a chance on the market. We know that the great break in the stock exchange in 1929 was caused mostly by the thousands, yes millions of people in north America who were trading on margin on the stock exchange. People trade on the grain exchange on margin, and the fluctuations in the market are such that the margins can be very quickly wiped out and people lose their all. The judgment of the general public is usually poor. When the Minister of Pensions (Mr. Power), speaking on the elections act said that you cannot take away judgment I thought of members of parliament receiving demands from different sections of their community for this, that or the other thing. One section of the community might demand the abolition of the grain exchange, and another section might say no, we want it, because we want to gamble on the exchange. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we should use our best judgment in whatever position we are placed; but the judgment of the public is usually poor; the element of chance makes a great appeal to them, and they will take a fling on the grain exchange to make some easy money. I see my friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are smiling, but really that is one of the great causes of the maldistribution of wealth. If we are to have a better distribution of wealth we must have in this country a system which will remove some of the causes of maldistribution, including gambling on the grain exchange.
Last summer, while I was in Great Britain, I observed that most of the millers buy their wheat on sample from the Liverpool shipping houses, and the transportation system over there is so different from what it used to be that the grain exchanges do not function as they formerly did. I am sure that this applies also to this country. Millers send their trucks right down to the boats, very frequently wheat taken from these ships is transported by road as far as Carlisle, on the borders of Scotland; it never gets on a train in passing from a boat to the mill, but is sold on sample at so much a ton, whether it be Argentine or Canadian or Australian wheat.
So to-day we are living under different conditions from those of the past. It has been said that everybody who speaks on this subject must have had his fingers burned. I 
do not think that is entirely true, but certainly we often have to learn from experience. Unfortunately the experience from which many have to learn is an experience of losses from which it is not they who suffer but those who are dependent upon them. So, if we wish to remove one definite blight upon society, I plead with this house to eliminate the waste of speculation in grain futures and so do something to raise the standard of living of our people.

I felt that since the bill follows out practically in their entirety the recommendations of the commissioner, Mr. Justice Turgeon, there is no real ground for believing that it is of a contentious nature. I do not think the question is whether we shall have an exchange or not; it is a matter of the regulation of the exchange. I shall not quote at any length from the report 71492-170
of the commissioner, because I assume that most hon. members have read it, but here are his words, at page 182:
In proceeding now to state the opinion I have formed regarding a marketing method for Canadian wheat, I shall first deal with the problem on the basis of normal conditions existing at home and abroad, that is conditions which do not call for action of an unusual nature involving a departure, more or less temporary, from settled and approved business practices.
And this is the sentence to which I would call attention:
Our policy should then be the continuation of the futures trading market at Winnipeg and the encouragement of the building up of producers' cooperative marketing societies, organized and conducted in a manner approaching in so far as practicable, the organization and business methods of the Australian pools. . . .
I shall not quote further at that particular point. After reviewing still further some of the considerations which determined his decision, the commissioner says:
Having regard to these considerations, I am convinced, from all the knowledge I have been able to acquire on the subject, that the futures trading system, despite its imperfections, is the one best qualified to look after the interests of our producers, at home and abroad.
Again he says:
It cannot be doubted that the closing of the Winnipeg exchange would greatly increase the volume of futures trading in our wheat in other markets, and the volume of speculation along with it. It is true that the Winnipeg market has not always been a fully satisfactory one. It has sometimes been out of line through causes which I have examined and which should be avoided in the future. Nevertheless I cannot help but feel that its closing would have a depressing effect upon our marketing, and would merely help to build up other markets without any corresponding advantage to ourselves. This was the effect of the prohibition, in 1896, of futures trading in Berlin.
Then he gives the experience of that exchange in Berlin. Sir Josiah Stamp submitted a report in connection with this very matter to which I have referred. At page 66 of his report he says:
The prohibition of business in options and futures (in Berlin) continued to paralyse business by making an effective insurance against loss extremely difficult, and at all events very expensive, because foreign markets such as New York and Chicago had to be resorted to.
And then he made this comment:
The produce exchange and dealing in options were shortly afterwards reopened.
Then he said that if the exchange were abolished altogether the only possible remedy would be the formation of a compulsory

Grain Futures

wheat board. I know very well that many of our western friends are in favour of a compulsory wheat board, but there are also a great many people in the west who are just as much opposed to it.

That is a matter of opinion which could not be proved. At any rate the commissioner makes this statement with reference to a wheat board. At the bottom of page 184 he says:
The demand made before me for the abolition of futures trading in Canada was always accompanied by a further demand for the creation by the government of a permanent national wheat board, whose duty it would be to take over the whole of our wheat crop each year and to market it both at home and abroad . . .
This proposal of a compulsory government board has preoccupied me more than anything else since the beginning of this inquiry. It was asked for by nearly all the farmers' organizations, and by a great many of the individual farmers, who appeared before me. It is a naturally attractive proposal at first blush, particularly after the many hard years our people have gone through. The idea of government support to marketing undoubtedly produces a sense of relief and security, and insufficient consideration is often given to the effect of such a policy on overseas importers. On the other hand, however, the feeling on the subject is by no means unanimous. Many fanners prefer to do their own marketing, and resent a compulsory taking over of their crop by a government board or any other organization. very few, I believe (if any), object to the operation of the present non-compulsory board created under the act of 1935.
I call attention especially to this.
Whatever attractions a compulsory government board may present at first sight, its practicability, in my opinion, will not stand analysis, either from the point of view of overseas markets or that of domestic conditions.
Then he quotes an authority who, I think, ought to appeal to my hon. friends opposite, particularly the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
The situation at home would also be disadvantageous to the producer, in my opinion. This opinion is held by many whose experience qualifies them to express well-considered views. Mr. John I. McFarland, who gave so much of his time and his ability to handling stabilization and who was the first chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, did not favour the closing of the Winnipeg exchange, nor did Mr. J. R. Murray, -who succeeded Mr. McFarland as chief commissioner.
Perhaps I have read enough to indicate that it was the very definite opinion of the commissioner, as stated in his report, that the Winnipeg exchange should remain open. He makes the suggestion embodied in the bill as to what supervision should be adopted in connection with the Winnipeg grain exchange, but I do not think it is necessary to read that.

What is given on the second page of the bill in the explanatory note is practically what the commissioner himself suggests.
My hon. friend objects to the wording "supervisor." I do not know exactly what official he would appoint. He mentioned some other name, but whether he would suggest that the supervisor should have any other duty than those given the official named in the bill, I was not able to gather.
I do not know that I can add anything further except to say that the bill is brought in as a direct recommendation of the commissioner who was appointed by parliament in 1936. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle made some criticism of the nature of the investigation undertaken by the commissioner. I would remind him that the report which recommended to parliament the appointment of a royal commission was the unanimous report of that committee of which he was himself a member.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I cannot exactly agree with that. There was really a minority report, because the second paragraph of the report indicates that the committee was not really unanimous and the suggestion was made accordingly that the matter should be referred to a commission.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE

Order. The hon. member has already spoken.

On section 2-Definitions.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
Have these definitions
been checked by reference to the authorities who constantly use the terms defined? For example, there is "cash grain." Is that the accepted term? If not, in what respect do these definitions vary from the terms in use?

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-Board of grain commissioners.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Has the minister considered giving the board of grain commissioners full control of the clearing house operations?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: The hon. member will find it in the bill.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I am referring to the supervising of the trade and so on.

Grain Futures

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend means by giving them complete control. It is not the purpose of the bill to interfere with the day-to-day transactions. It is merely to supervise operations, and should anything take place that is regarded as prejudicial to the interests of the grain trade, they have the power to intervene. That is as far as we are supposed to go.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: How far will the board have power to go with respect to rules and regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I can answer that question when we come to the section covering it.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Who are the members of the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: There are three members: Mr. Ramsay, the chairman; Mr. Hamilton, and Doctor MacGibbon.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-Supervisor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Subsection 1 provides that the governor in council may appoint a qualified person to be the supervisor, and that the supervisor shall be an officer of the board, shall hold office during pleasure and shall receive such salary as may be fixed by the governor in council. It does not even say "on the recommendation of the board of grain commissioners." Should not this supervisor be recommended by the board? It seems to me that would be better than to leave it to the governor in council. On whose recommendation will the governor in council act?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
Of course the governor in
council must take the responsibility for the appointment in any event.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I appreciate that, but if
they put the responsibility on the board of grain commissioners they would be on pretty solid ground. Supposing they chose to appoint someone whom the board- of grain commissioners did not approve. It seems to me the board which is possessed of such great powers, even to the extent of supervising trading on the Winnipeg grain exchange, should have the duty of recommending this man. I am not going to argue the point, but that seems to me the logical procedure. By whom is this person to be recommended? I think the minister would be protecting himself and the government by making it compulsory for the board of grain commissioners to recommend the supervisor.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
7X492-170J
On section 5-Regulations.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I must confess that I do
not know very much about the grain business or the growing of grain, so it is merely in order to obtain some information that I ask this question. Is it the intention under this bill to supervise transactions on the Winnipeg grain exchange only? Are there not other exchanges in other parts of Canada where business in grain is transacted?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
Not in the same way; and
there is provision that if in future there should be such exchanges, they will be subject to this bill just as the Winnipeg grain exchange is.	'

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
Under this section we
have the powers of the board outlined. Has any question been raised by interested parties as to the extent of these powers? They are extremely broad, and they are not defined in the bill, which says:
The board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, make regulations not inconsistent with this act-
Then it enumerates the classifications of those regulations, but the bill itself does not outline the principles that should restrain the board. It seems to me that under this section they might pass almost any regulation they wished.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
But their regulations are
subject to the approval of the governor in council.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Yes, but that is not legislative control. To put it bluntly, this might be used as a powerful political weapon. It is open to that. It might be used as a regimenting instrument. I am not saying that is the intention, but I am pointing out that in my opinion the bill itself should lay down the principles the board must follow. As it is at the present time, this has no meaning or force, because the board may make almost any regulations it wishes, subject to the approval of the governor in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
With all due deference to my hon. friend I would think that the principles were pretty well laid down here. I think my hon. friend will also admit, from his experience in the framing of statutes, that in most statutes provision is made to permit the minister to frame regulations under which the work shall be carried on. That is precisely what is being done here. As to just what the regulations may be, I cannot say; nor would I say that it would be proper-perhaps it would not be improper-to put the regulations themselves into the statute. I do not think my hon. friend would suggest that.
Grain Futures

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
No. Let me illustrate what I mean. This section reads:
(X) The board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, make regulations not inconsistent with this act,-
(b) requiring the Winnipeg grain exchange and the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Exchange Clearing Association Limited and the members of each of the said associations to keep such records relating to trading in grain futures on the Winnipeg grain exchange as are specified by such regulations-*
Just follow that language; the board may make regulations not inconsistent with the act, such as are specified iby such regulations. That is the language. The bill does not lay down the basis of the regulations in respect of this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: It says " to keep records."

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: But the regulation may call for any class of records at all. There should be some limitation to which the board should be subject, or there should be some broad principles laid down. I know what they are driving at here, but this bill does not give the faintest intimation of it. They may call upon these people to produce records of any kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: If I may interrupt, they are only empowered to call for records dealing with trading in grain futures.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Certainly; but as the Minister of Mines and Resources knows very well from his experience, that covers practically all the dealings of the members of the grain exchange.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: In grain futures.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Which touches virtually all the business of most of their members. This does not indicate the class of records or the limitation beyond which the board may not go. I am not going to labour the point, but I think it is .my duty to indicate that the bill does not lay down principles which will guide the board, but rather gives the board wide-open power to call for any records or any class of records they may desire.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I would submit to the committee and to my hon. friend that the principle is laid down when it is stated that the board may demand that records ibe kept. As to the extent or minuteness to which those records may be asked for, that is a matter of regulation. I think in all legislation of this kind, where you empower an organization or a government body to carry on certain duties, you must have some confidence that they are going to exercise a certain degree of common sense. If they did not, I should imagine any government would think they were not fit for

the job and would find someone else to do it.
I do think the principle is laid down when you say they shall keep records. I would submit that it would not be proper to include in the bill in great detail exactly what sort of records should be kept.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
This bill is really the result of a recommendation by a committee of this house that a royal grain commission be appointed. A few moments ago the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said that 'the report of the committee was not unanimous I was a member of the subcommittee that drew up that report; the then right hon. leader of the opposition, Mr. Bennett, was another member, and we were in complete agreement as to the report that was made to the main committee. That main committee recommended the setting up of a royal commission to go into many different features of the grain trade, and I think the grain trade was thoroughly covered by the commission that was appointed.
This bill simply places upon the Winnipeg grain exchange a supervisor to watch the transactions of the traders and to see, if possible, that no action is taken by the traders on that exchange that is disadvantageous to the producers or handlers of grain throughout this country. In dealing with grain matters in this house over a great many years we have found it pretty hard to frame any measure tight enough to hold the traders in grain, so I do not think the hon. member for Kootenay East need worry about putting through a bill giving too many powers to a supervisor or to the board under which he works.
We have had at times to use acts other than the grain act to try to control the handling of grain in Canada. This supervisor is properly put under the board of grain commissioners who handle the regulation of the whole grain trade of Canada, and he should have the right to look into all the records of the traders in grain on the Winnipeg grain exchange. They should be made, as under this measure, to keep proper records of all their trading, so that through the board of grain commissioners and the supervisor, the government, when necessaiy, can control the trading on that grain exchange. I do not think it is necessary to send the bill to the committee on agriculture. There is only one purpose behind the bill, namely, that of placing a supervisor over the Winnipeg grain exchange to watch over the transactions gone into by grain traders, and to see that no trading of any kind takes place which will take advantage of the producer in the handling of grain as it goes on the market.

Grain Futures

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: In reply to the hon. member may I say I think we can settle once and for all the matter with respect to unanimity in connection with the report. I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce was chairman of that committee. The hon. member will recall the report of the subcommittee as it was first brought in. Although I have not the report before me, still I can recollect the main paragraph. It was stated first of all that while there was a short interest on December 13, I believe it was, on the Winnipeg grain exchange, no evidence was produced which would warrant the conclusion that the shorts had been protected by the board. That was the way it read. The subcommittee was asked to consider that matter. It will be recalled that the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, who was a member of the committee, and one or two others including myself, objected to stopping there. The report was more or less a compromise. As it now stands, it is a negative-positive report. We agreed to it, but it must be remembered that it contained the words that as the committee found it impracticable to get conclusive evidence on the point as to whether or not shorts were protected, they suggested that it be referred to a commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: That was unanimous.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Yes, but I point out to this committee that it was a compromise.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: All unanimous reports must be a compromise.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: But I must say it was a compromise report, even at that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Shall section 5 carry?

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: No. I have in mind regulations which I believe might come under paragraph (el of section 5. I would suggest there should be some provisions whereby the supervisor could make public or would publish at the close of any session during the calendar year the exact standing in the clearing house of shorts and longs, possibly of some of the traders over a certain limit.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I think he has the power to do that under the bill.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: He should have power to make known the exact position at the close of each session.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I do not suppose he would be precluded. He can do it by regulation.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I think that is an important point, and it should be embodied in the bill under paragraph (e) or (f). Paragraph (f) does not go as far as I should like
the supervisor to go. I think he should have power to publish at the close of each session during the calendar year, if he so desires, the exact standings as to shorts and longs and hedges in the clearing house.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: The supervisor would not have that power in any event; he only makes investigations. It is the board that would have to take action. However, I do not see anything in the bill which would preclude the board from publishing the information to which the hon. member refers, if they thought it well to do so. I do not think it should be included definitely as a command or instruction which they must carry out.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I would point out to the minister that probably he is wrong there. That is why I was saying a moment ago that it would be better to indicate in the measure the general lines the regulation should take. Then that creates a power. Making a regulation is simply giving effect to legislative powers. There is no legislative power given here to publish a daily record of longs and shorts, such as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has mentioned. And I question if the mere right to make regulations confers that power. We should have had the Minister of Justice or some other of the legal advisers in the government to give an opinion on the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member. Would he look at paragraph (f).

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I have seen it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
It states:
(f) providing for the publication by the board of information and statistics relating to the marketing of grain.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
But "information and
statistics relating to the marketing of grain" would not authorize or empower this board to force a private operator to disclose his private business. I venture to say no court would uphold the board in endeavouring, as the bill now stands, to force such trader to do so. Statistics and information regarding marketing embody only the normal information given the public from day to day. I refer to the price of grain, the unloadings, the amounts in elevators and all that sort of thing. It refers to the regular written statistics.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: He must give particulars of his transactions in grain futures, and that is open to inspection of the supervisor.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I shall not labour the
point. But I emphasize again it would be better if the bill indicated clearly the general
Grain Futures

lines of information and the general powers the board should exercise, and upon which it would base its regulations.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: On that point may I say that I believe under this measure the board have power to do all that it is necessary to do. When the hon. member says that they should have power to show the open interest, the longs and shorts on the market, may I say that ordinarily that is published by the trade. One can get that information with respect to the Chicago market. I have got it for years; it is published every day in the newspapers. But when you come to showing the amount of open interest, either long or short, that any individual has, then surely if you are going to operate a government grain board under the act you do not want published the figures showing the amount of grain that board has, or the amount of grain they are dealing in on any day. That is one of the things you must, if possible, keep from the trade. I do not think we should put things into the measure, without very serious consideration as to what effect they would have. I think the bill is properly drawn, and that wide enough powers are given to the board and the supervisor to get the information necessary for him to have to supervise the exchange.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
I do not think that under
paragraph (f) the supervisor has the power we think he should have. We are led to believe that last fall there was a selling pressure on the market. Very much more was being sold every day than there was cash wheat or wheat that was being delivered to the interior elevators throughout the west.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Selling pressure by whom?

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: By the "big three," international grain firms.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: When did they buy it back?

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
Maybe they have not bought it back yet, and are depending on getting wheat from the board. Probably they got a great deal of wheat in December to fill their contracts. If the supervisor at the close of each session had power to make public the short and long interest; if, as I said when speaking earlier this evening, the buying and selling hedges had been balanced, and if it was apparent that there was a very great majority of sales, over and above purchases,
I think-

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
How can there
be a sale without a buyer?

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: A man may sell without having cash wheat to deliver on the option.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Somebody has to take up the contract to buy.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Somebody else has to take the contract for the wheat. There is short selling by operators. True enough, someone has to buy the option, but they sold wheat when they never had any cash wheat to deliver, expecting to get it from the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Who bought it?

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Possibly the minister bought some on speculation, possibly myself or others.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I believe section 5 confers the powers asked for by the hon. member foi Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). Paragraphs (b), (c) and (f) must be taken together. Paragraph (b) requires the Winnipeg grain exchange to keep records of trading in grain futures. Paragraph (c) requires the grain exchange to furnish to the board or to the supervisor the information specified in the regulations relating to grain futures. Paragraph (f) provides for the publication of such information by the board. In my opinion these three paragraphs grant the powers requested by the hon. member.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
Is there anything under
section 5 which would give the supervisor power to regulate the amount of hedging which could be carried on as against cash wheat? Is there anything which provides that a member of the exchange cannot sell, say more than two or three times the amount of cash wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE

speechtext:
Section agreed to.

and they are hereby further amended by inserting immediately after subsection 2 of section VIII-grain products-the following subsection, to be numbered 2A:-
2A. Flour shall be the fine, clean sound product made by the milling of wheat and shall contain not more than thirteen and five-tenths parts (13-5) per cent of moisture, not less than one and twenty-five hundredths parts (1-25) per cent of organic nitrogen, not more than one part (1) per cent of ash, and not more than five-tenths of one part (0-5) per cent of fibre, with or without the addition of non-injurious ingredients for modifying the colour or baking qualities; provided that, in the case of the addition of non-injurious ingredients, there shall be stated clearly and conspicuously upon the labels of all packages containing flour so modified, "This flour contains improvers."
The order in council to which objection was taken last year has been modified to cover labeling where non-injurious ingredients other than those specified in the definition are added to flour.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Has the department taken any action to classify improvers? For instance, is it now possible to use potassium bromate?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE

speechtext:

the department with respect to bleaching or colouring agents?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: There is a definition stating what shall go into flour, and if anything else is used they must say "improvers added."

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Is Canadian flour sent abroad containing these ingredients to which reference has just been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Not without labeling.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Do we send adulterated flour abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
No. We do not send
adulterated flour anywhere. My hon. friend and some others have been very anxious to spread abroad and in Canada the idea that we have been adulterating flour. We have not been adulterating flour at any time, and the hon. gentlemen who have got into the habit of saying that, are not doing any good either to Canada or to themselves. They are far from the truth in the first place.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
But it is possible, according to the return, on the evidence given by the officers of the minister's own department, to achieve the same results by the proper blending of grains, such as the introduction of No. 1 northern. By permitting the use of synthetic improvers in Canadian flours for export abroad, we are damaging our export
Supply-National Health

trade and encouraging among the millers in Great Britain and France a practice that hitherto has been frowned upon by health authorities in Great Britain and other European countries. Why not establish definite standards of purity for Canadian flour to encourage millers abroad to use larger quantities of No. 1?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: Why does not my hon. friend read carefully or state accurately the documents which we brought down for him? He knows very well that we produced everything we had in the department, something I believe no other minister ever did, confidential documents, reports from our own officers and everything else, in order that he might have all the facts and not go about, making the statements he did make all summer. In England they do permit the use of improvers, and my hon. friend knows it if he read the file at all. I took the trouble to inquire from the Department of Trade and Commerce whether the use of improvers would have any injurious effect on No. 1 flour, and the officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce and of the wheat board said no. So why should my hon. friend state in this chamber something that is absolutely contrary to the facts as set out in the file?

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I still submit that the file shows clearljr that in Great Britain the health authorities are bringing pressure to bear on the trade to adopt wherever possible physical rather than chemical processes to improve the quality of flour. It was pointed out that the results sought could be achieved by the proper blending of grains in Canada and by allowing the flour to mature in storage.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: In Great Britain they have the right to add improvers to flour. That is all stated in the file. So why should my hon. friend come here and tell us differently?

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I am not disputing that statement, but I do say that the health authorities in Great Britain brought pressure to bear on the trade, and that is shown on the file.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: That is not what the hon. member said in the first place.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: It is exactly. I did not say that it was prohibited in Great Britain, but in certain European countries it is prohibited. The health authorities in Great Britain have indicated that the government there was giving leadership to the trade, and encouraging in every way possible the development of a fine quality of flour by physical rather than by chemical processes.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: And permitting the use of improvers in the flour.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I am not saying they are prohibited, but I say that it would be well in Canada as a matter of policy to encourage the blending of grains and the maturing of flour in storage, to get the finest quality of flour by the use of physical rather than chemical processes.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport

speechtext: This deals with the maintenance of small wharves operated under the Harbours and Piers Act. It covers all wharves except harbours board wharves and one or two other wharves that are operated under a separate act.

maintopic: SUPERVISION AND REGULATION OP TRADING IN FUTURES ON WINNIPEG GRAIN EXCHANGE
speechtext: I should like to know the results of the minister's investigations. I have brought to his attention several matters with regard to wharfingers at small wharves along the coast of British Columbia. The imposition of top wharfage tolls has meant a great inconvenience to members of the community who must depend upon these wharves as providing the only communication with the outside world. Returns have been tabled this session indicating that wharfingers have been appointed at some wharves and not at others a short distance away. There is discrimination. Apparently there has been complete absence of control by the department over many of these wharves. As a result of personal investigation I find that in many instances fishermen who are supposed to be exempt from wharfage tolls are charged fifty cents for a tie-up when in distress. That is contrary to the provisions of the act and is a grave abuse which should be checked by the department. I have brought a number of these matters to the attention of the department in the hope of having them investigated. What exactly is the procedure in respect to auditing receipts of top wharfage tolls at these wharves?
